Convergence of the chains

Muhammad Yaseen

2026-11-05

Source: vignettes/bayesammi_05_convergence.qmd

\[ \newcommand{\vy}{\mathbf{y}} \newcommand{\vx}{\mathbf{x}} \newcommand{\vb}{\mathbf{b}} \newcommand{\ve}{\mathbf{e}} \newcommand{\vone}{\mathbf{1}} \newcommand{\vbeta}{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \newcommand{\vmu}{\boldsymbol{\mu}} \newcommand{\mX}{\mathbf{X}} \newcommand{\mZ}{\mathbf{Z}} \newcommand{\mV}{\mathbf{V}} \newcommand{\mI}{\mathbf{I}} \newcommand{\mJ}{\mathbf{J}} \newcommand{\mSigma}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}} \newcommand{\mY}{\mathbf{Y}} \newcommand{\mK}{\mathbf{K}} \newcommand{\mH}{\mathbf{H}} \newcommand{\va}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} \newcommand{\vg}{\boldsymbol{\gamma}} \newcommand{\vt}{\boldsymbol{\tau}} \newcommand{\vd}{\boldsymbol{\delta}} \newcommand{\vtheta}{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \newcommand{\vv}{\mathbf{v}} \newcommand{\E}{\mathrm{E}} \newcommand{\Var}{\mathrm{Var}} \newcommand{\Cov}{\mathrm{Cov}} \newcommand{\tr}{\operatorname{tr}} \]

1 Abstract

Posterior summaries are valid only after the chains have reached their stationary distribution and are long enough. Crossa et al. (2011) used three diagnostics: Raftery and Lewis (1995), Heidelberger and Welch (1983) and Gelman and Rubin (1992). bayes_ammi() computes all three, together with effective sample sizes, through the package coda.

2 Several chains 

fit <-
  bayes_ammi(
      .data   = Maiz
    , .y      = y
    , .gen    = entry
    , .env    = site
    , .rep    = rep
    , .nIter  = 4000
    , .k      = 2
    , .burnin = 1000
    , .thin   = 1
    , .chains = 3
    , .priors = bam_priors(
          mu_mean     = 0
        , mu_var      = 1e+8
        , tau_mean    = 0
        , tau_var     = 1e+8
        , delta_mean  = 0
        , delta_var   = 1e+8
        , lambda_mean = 0
        , lambda_var  = 1e+8
        , nu          = 1
        , s2          = NULL
        )
    , .level  = 0.95
    , .seed   = 5
    , .align  = TRUE
    , .model  = "AMMI"
    , .het    = FALSE
    , .waic   = TRUE
    )

The first chain starts at the least-squares fit and the others at dispersed values (singular values scaled by factors between 0.5 and 1.5, perturbed scores, error variance scaled between 0.5 and 2).

3 Traces 

plot(x = fit, which = "trace", pars = c("mu", "sigma2", "lambda[1]", "lambda[2]", "alpha[8,1]"))

4 Gelman-Rubin

The potential scale reduction factor compares the variance between chains with the variance within them. Values below 1.1 (better, 1.01) indicate that the chains have mixed.

5 Raftery-Lewis

The dependence factor \(I\) measures how much longer the chain must be than an independent sample of the same precision; \(I > 5\) indicates strong autocorrelation.

6 Heidelberger-Welch

The stationarity test is applied to the whole chain, then after dropping the first 10%, 20%, … of it. The half-width test asks whether the mean is estimated precisely enough. Each test has level 0.05, so among many parameters a few failures are expected by chance.

7 Effective sample size and Monte Carlo error 

fit$summary[block %in% c("mu", "sigma2", "lambda"), list(parameter, mean, sd, mc_se, ess, rhat)]
   parameter       mean         sd       mc_se       ess      rhat
      <char>      <num>      <num>       <num>     <num>     <num>
1:        mu   4857.976    32.5537   0.2925239 12384.485 0.9999954
2:    sigma2 763066.073 43412.8267 500.5970862  7520.721 1.0002382
3: lambda[1]   5468.348   457.4447   4.6530521  9664.991 1.0003939
4: lambda[2]   1654.395   784.8158  21.0012922  1396.508 1.0000922

The Monte Carlo standard error mc_se is \(\mathrm{sd}/\sqrt{\mathrm{ess}}\). Run longer chains when it is not small compared with the precision you need. The weak second singular value mixes more slowly than the other parameters.

8 The draws for further analysis

fit$draws is a coda::mcmc.list, so every function of coda applies:

coda::autocorr.diag(mcmc.obj = fit$draws[, c("lambda[1]", "lambda[2]")], lags = c(1, 5, 10))
        lambda[1] lambda[2]
Lag 1  0.08931897 0.7099201
Lag 5  0.02070703 0.3129273
Lag 10 0.01404242 0.1274023

9 posterior and bayesplot

The draws also convert to a draws_df of posterior, which gives the rank-normalised \(\widehat{R}\) and the bulk and tail effective sample sizes of Vehtari et al. (2021), and the plots of bayesplot take the mcmc.list directly (Gabry et al. 2019):

dr <- posterior::as_draws_df(x = fit)
posterior::summarise_draws(
    .x = posterior::subset_draws(x = dr, variable = c("mu", "sigma2", "lambda[1]", "lambda[2]"))
  , "mean", "sd", "rhat", "ess_bulk", "ess_tail"
  )
# A tibble: 4 × 6
  variable     mean      sd  rhat ess_bulk ess_tail
  <chr>       <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>
1 mu          4858.    32.6  1.00   11956.   12016.
2 sigma2    763066. 43413.   1.00    6507.    9830.
3 lambda[1]   5468.   457.   1.00    9062.   10658.
4 lambda[2]   1654.   785.   1.01    1242.    3663.
bayesplot::mcmc_rank_overlay(x = fit$draws, pars = c("lambda[1]", "lambda[2]"))

Rank plots are flat and overlapping when the chains mix well.

10 Interpretation of convergence 

bam_interpret(
    x             = fit
  , higher_better = TRUE
  , top           = 5
  )$findings[1:2]
[1] "The chains have converged by the criteria of Crossa et al. (2011) (largest potential scale reduction factor 1.001); the smallest effective sample size of the main parameters is 1,400."
[2] "6 of 198 Heidelberger-Welch stationarity and half-width tests failed (about 5% fail by chance at level 0.05)."

11 References

Crossa, J., Perez-Elizalde, S., Jarquin, D., Cotes, J. M., Viele, K., Liu, G. and Cornelius, P. L. (2011). Bayesian estimation of the additive main effects and multiplicative interaction model. Crop Science, 51(4), 1458–1469. doi:10.2135/cropsci2010.06.0343

Gelman, A. and Rubin, D. B. (1992). Inference from iterative simulation using multiple sequences. Statistical Science, 7(4), 457–472.

Raftery, A. E. and Lewis, S. M. (1995). The number of iterations, convergence diagnostics and generic Metropolis algorithms. In W. R. Gilks, D. J. Spiegelhalter and S. Richardson (eds), Practical Markov Chain Monte Carlo. Chapman and Hall, London.

Heidelberger, P. and Welch, P. D. (1983). Simulation run length control in the presence of an initial transient. Operations Research, 31(6), 1109–1144.

Plummer, M., Best, N., Cowles, K. and Vines, K. (2006). CODA: convergence diagnosis and output analysis for MCMC. R News, 6(1), 7–11.

Vehtari, A., Gelman, A., Simpson, D., Carpenter, B. and Burkner, P.-C. (2021). Rank-normalization, folding, and localization: an improved R-hat for assessing convergence of MCMC. Bayesian Analysis, 16(2), 667–718.

Gabry, J., Simpson, D., Vehtari, A., Betancourt, M. and Gelman, A. (2019). Visualization in Bayesian workflow. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society A, 182(2), 389–402.
